title: Lamb Tagine
subtitle: Moroccan slow-braised lamb with preserved lemon and olives
excerpt: A Moroccan tagine is a slow braise named after the earthenware vessel it is traditionally cooked in. This lamb version uses ras el hanout, saffron, and preserved lemon -- the defining flavours of Moroccan cooking. It is patient cooking with a spectacular result.
sourceNotes: Tagine has been central to Moroccan cooking for over a thousand years. The conical clay pot allows steam to circulate and condense, keeping meat moist during the long braise. Preserved lemon and olives are the signature finishing ingredients of a lamb tagine.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze after cooking, without the preserved lemon rind. Add fresh lemon when reheating.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Tastes better the next day. Make up to 2 days ahead and reheat gently.

content.text: If you have a traditional tagine pot, use it. If not, a heavy casserole dish works well. The key is a tight lid and a low oven. Do not rush the braise.

items.prepNote: use 1.5 tsp ras el hanout spice blend
use 1 preserved lemon, rind only, finely chopped

content.text: Preheat the oven to 160 degrees. Heat the oil in a heavy casserole over high heat. Brown the lamb in batches until dark on all sides. Remove and set aside.
Reduce the heat to medium. Cook the onion in the same pot for 8 minutes until soft and golden.
Add the garlic and ginger. Cook for 2 minutes. Add the ras el hanout and turmeric. Stir for 1 minute.
Return the lamb to the pot. Pour in the stock and saffron water. Season with salt. Bring to a simmer.
Cover tightly and transfer to the oven. Cook for 90 minutes until the lamb is completely tender.
Stir in the preserved lemon rind and green olives. Return to the oven uncovered for 10 minutes.
Rest for 10 minutes. Serve with couscous or flatbread.

items.symptom: Lamb is still tough after 90 minutes
items.cause: Oven too low, or the shoulder pieces were very large
items.fix: Cook for another 20 minutes -- lamb shoulder needs a long slow braise
Remove the lamb and simmer the sauce on the hob to reduce

items.cause: Preserved lemon rind was not rinsed before adding
items.fix: Always rinse preserved lemon under cold water before use, and taste before adding the olives which also add salt

content.text: Tagine is the everyday dish of Morocco. It is cooked in homes, sold in medina restaurants, and served at family celebrations. The lamb and preserved lemon version is perhaps the most classic. Fez and Marrakech both claim definitive versions. Ras el hanout -- meaning head of the shop -- is the signature spice blend, and no two spice merchants make it exactly the same way.
